risks.note: As an intermediary, the trading business earns margin on the purchase-sale spread, which narrows quickly when raw material or freight costs rise faster than customers will absorb, making profitability more sensitive to market swings than manufacturers with pricing control.

Sourcing from external suppliers under the trading model means limited control over product availability, lead times and quality consistency; any disruption at the supplier's end directly affects the ability to fulfil customer commitments.
Trading businesses compete on price in a market where customers can compare multiple suppliers easily, limiting pricing power and making customer retention harder without added service value.

Trading operations require holding inventory and extending credit to customers while managing supplier payment terms, creating working capital pressure sensitive to receivables cycles and interest-rate movements.

Where sourcing involves imported goods, the business is exposed to currency fluctuations, freight rate volatility and shipping disruptions, which can affect landed cost and delivery timelines beyond its direct control.
A moderating global economy, energy price volatility and shifting trade patterns create external risk to demand and input costs.
Establishing and scaling a new manufacturing facility at Suwana carries project execution, technology adoption and market-entry risk for a Company historically focused on trading.
